extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of journalism, media scholars, newspaper editors and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for assessing newspapers and newsgathering: what counts as news, how economic structures shape editorial choices, and the limits and reliability of reporting. Useful for evaluating journalism quality and designing news organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of a 'free and truthful' press
rubrics_metrics.description: It is practically universally assumed that the press should be 'free' and 'truthful' and that the newspaper will present a true picture of the outer world for readers without their actively contracting for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect news 'gratis' and do not enter into contracts that share the cost or risk of newsgathering. This cultural expectation shapes the economics and moral judgments applied to newspapers (they are ethically judged like churches or schools even though they operate under different financial arrangements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic model determines editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation is an asset only when it can be sold to advertisers; advertisers buy space in publications that reach their future customers, so newspapers tend to respect the point of view of the buying public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because newspapers rely on indirect revenues (advertising) rather than direct payment by readers, editorial choices are influenced by who advertisers wish to reach. Alienating the buying public risks losing the indispensable asset for survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of circulation (quality vs mass) matters to advertisers
rubrics_metrics.description: The kind of circulation the advertiser will buy depends on what he has to sell; circulation that reaches the fairly prosperous (neither the very rich nor the very poor) is most valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical advertising agents distinguish 'quality' and 'mass' circulation; the value of a newspaper's circulation is judged by its fit with advertisers' target customers and may vary by product line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader loyalty (constancy) as a source of independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A devoted band of constant readers gives a newspaper the greatest practical independence possible under modern economics; loyalty can be more powerful than any single advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since most readers do not pay enough or commit long-term, the editor must cultivate loyalty through content. When readers will 'stay by it through thick and thin' they can counter combinations of advertisers and protect editorial autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers judge newspapers by coverage of personally relevant events
rubrics_metrics.description: Most readers tend to judge a newspaper by its treatment of that part of the news in which they feel themselves involved — their business, church, party, or local affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the newspaper 'gives a satisfactory account' of events readers know from their own experience, it is likely to win trust and be immune from violent criticism by those readers; this predisposes selection toward local/personal items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal constraints shape what can be reported (libel/slander)
rubrics_metrics.description: General readers have no standing in law to sue for misleading news; only aggrieved parties can sue for slander or libel and must prove material injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of libel laws and legal risk, newspapers are constrained from publishing mere rumors or unverifiable private information; definitive, objectified facts (public records, overt acts) are safer to report.

rubrics_metrics.name: News requires overt, objectified acts to be reportable
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a series of events become news they usually have to make themselves noticeable in some more or less overt act — bankruptcy filings, arrests, speeches, votes, bills introduced, fires, collisions, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rumors or background knowledge without a definable public manifestation cannot safely be published as news. Reporters rely on public acts and records to 'uncover' news; the more definite the act, the more reportable it is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of news correlates with existence of record machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is a good machinery of record (stock exchange tickers, election tabulation, civil registration of births/deaths/marriages), the news service works with great precision; where records lack, news is debatable or neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess news reliability by checking whether the topic passes through official or standardized recording systems. Topics without such systems (internal trade over the counter, states of mind, motives) are inherently less certain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of reporting on states of mind, motives, and mass feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: All news about states of mind, descriptions of personalities, motives, intentions, mass feeling, public opinion and similar subjects are of a character where the data are spasmodically recorded or not recorded at all, so reporting is debatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should treat such material as provisional, often expressed as opinions, or seek investigatory work that objectifies the matter; avoid presenting such subjects as precise factual certainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on institutional beats and standardized routines
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters cannot be everywhere; they 'watch' certain institutional places (Police Headquarters, County Clerk's Office, City Hall, the White House, legislative chambers) or rely on associations that monitor these places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsgathering is routinized and location-based. Evaluate coverage by considering which beats exist and how effectively reporters monitor these institutional sources for overt acts and records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agents filter and shape information reaching the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized groups hire press agents who act as intermediaries between organizations (corporations, banks, railroads, political groups, statesmen) and newspapers; many direct channels to news are closed and first filtered through publicity agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of information that arrives via press agents; recognize the strategic position of publicity intermediaries and corroborate with independent sources or public records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic undervaluing of straight reporting undermines professional standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting (the foundation of the institution) is the most poorly paid and least regarded branch of newspaper work; able people often treat reporting as temporary, limiting the development of corporate traditions and professional pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional health by examining career structures and compensation for reporters; stronger professional incentives and traditions foster higher standards of admission, self-discipline, and craft pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial content mix shaped by need to retain readers rather than by news importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because general political and social news does not alone secure large steady readerships, newspapers include features (society pages, scandal, sports, comics, advice columns, women's pages, cooking, puzzles) primarily designed to hold readers together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many editorial choices are driven by audience-retention economics. A paper's emphasis on soft features or sensational items may reflect survival strategy more than an editorial judgment of public importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: News is selective — not a mirror of social conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first instance, the news is not a mirror of social conditions but the report of aspects that have obtruded themselves; events must assume a certain definable shape before they separate from the 'ocean of possible truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interrogate claims of comprehensive coverage. Understand that selection bias is inherent: news reports what becomes manifest and recorded, not necessarily what is most important in underlying processes.
